sources.headline: Krakow shooting suspect has died in hospital, police say
sources.text: A gunman suspected of killing six people in central Krakow, as well as his parents and sister at their home, died in hospital early on Monday, Polish police have said.The 24-year-old, who has been named as Michal Oksinski by local media, was injured after opening fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland, on Saturday, police said.Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the suspect, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.Authorities initially reported that the gunman had apparently been inspired by "far-right ideologies", but have since said they are investigating any possible motivation.After the shooting, which began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's busy Main Market Square, police identified the attacker as a 24-year-old Polish man. In the hours after the shooting, a minister said that early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.However, during a press briefing on Monday morning, Przemysław Nowak, a spokesperson for Poland's National Prosecutor's Office, said investigations into his motive remain ongoing.Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed in the attack.Four victims are Polish, while a British national and an Austrian woman were also killed.Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three bodies - two women and one man - were found at the gunman's house when it was searched after the attack.On Sunday, Polish police confirmed those three victims had been identified as the alleged gunman's 53-year-old father, 52-year-old mother and 21-year-old sister.Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.Four firearms were found in the gunman's car, including two AR-15 rifles and two handguns, along with several hundred rounds of ammunition, Nowak said. Authorities also seized at least four phones from his car and person, and electronic equipment from his home.Sixteen people, including five foreigners, two police officers and the attacker, were taken to hospital. The interior ministry later said they were from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia.Speaking on Sunday, one of two surgeons who treated victims on the street after the attack said his colleague "undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.The two surgeons, who were eating near the Main Market Square when the gunman opened fire, rushed to the scene to treat both the attacker and the two injured police officers. Professor Michal Pędziwiatr told the BBC: "We saw the shooting attack. And what a surgeon can do in a situation like this?... We decided to help the victims as soon as possible.""We rushed into the area where the shooting was and started our rescue, because there were no ambulances available, there were no professionals around."Pędziwiatr said his colleague, who has been named by local media as Dr Mateusz Wierdak, used his hand to stem the bleeding from the most severely injured policeman, allowing time for an ambulance to arrive.On Sunday it was reported that both injured officers had emerged from comas.Witnesses who were near the Main Market Square have described their panic and confusion as the attack unfolded. Ruby, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives".She said they "just kept sprinting" until they found a hotel to shelter inside. Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover"."I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 metres away," he said.

sources.headline: Polish prosecutors say ‘too early’ to tell if Kraków gunman was motivated by political ideology
sources.text: Polish prosecutors have said they do not currently have any evidence tying the man who killed six people and injured 16 in a rare mass shooting in Kraków to any particularly political ideology.The 24-year-old Polish national died in hospital early on Monday after being critically injured in a shootout with police officers as they apprehended him after the attack in the city’s busy market square on Saturday afternoon.Soon after the attack, the bodies of the gunman’s parents and sister were found at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a town about 100 miles north-east of Kraków. Police said they had probably died of gunshot wounds.Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said on Saturday that the gunman, named in multiple reports as Michał Oksiński, was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views.CCTV footage shows police shootout after Kraków attack – videoPolish prosecutors opened a terrorism investigation, which the justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, said would continue despite the gunman’s death and would aim to establish if he had acted alone or had been inspired by any group.However, at a press conference on Monday, prosecutors said there was no evidence tying the suspect to any particular political bent.“We do not have findings that we could, in a responsible way, categorically state that he was inspired by any particular ideology,” said the national prosecutor’s office spokesperson, Przemysław Nowak.“It is far too early to comment on the motives … We have not found any obvious symbols that are generally associated with a particular political movement, whether far right or far left,” he added.An interior ministry spokesperson told Polish radio that the “many emblems and patches” on Oksiński’s clothing were being analysed as part of the investigation.A view of the empty square after the attack. Photograph: Omar Marques/Getty ImagesŻurek also called for “restraint” earlier on Monday amid the ongoing investigation. “Evidence is ​being collected, ​but I will not ​show or disclose it. I ask for restraint,” he told Radio ‌Zet.Candles and flowers are placed in the market square in Kraków after the shooting. Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/ReutersWearing military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest, the gunman drove at high speed into the square in the heart of the old town, which is usually packed with tourists, and started shooting at random in a “wild ride” around the square, the Kraków police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło said.A bullet hole at the scene of the shooting. Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty ImagesThe shooting has shocked a country that had been considered safer than many of its European neighbours, and has deepened concern after several school stabbings in October that left one woman dead and which officials said were linked to extremist content online.Among the six victims were a 32-year-old British man and an Austrian woman aged 51. The other four victims were Polish nationals.Of the 16 injured, 15 were in a stable condition as of late on Sunday, including two police officers who were brought out of medically induced comas earlier in the day. Five of the injured were from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia.Chairs lie scattered across a cafe terrace in the square the day after the shootings. Photograph: Beata Zawrzel/APPolice said the suspect, who had no criminal record and held a firearms licence, initially continued shooting even after he was wounded by police during the exchange of fire. The two injured police officers – Jakub Kulik, a former paratrooper and volunteer firefighter, and Artur Morański– were hailed as heroes for their rapid response and for preventing further casualties.Police confirmed on Sunday that three people found dead at the gunman’s home were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21.Mourners have left candles in tribute to the victims in the square, which reopened late on Sunday. Flags across the country were lowered to half mast during two days of national mourning, as were European flags outside the European Commission in Brussels “in solidarity with the Polish people”, the commission said.

sources.headline: Mass Killing in Poland Becomes Cause for a Political Fight
sources.text: The government blames the far right for inspiring the gunman, while the opposition accuses the government of lax security.

sources.headline: Krakow mass shooting suspect has died in hospital, police in Poland say
sources.text:
The alleged shooter who went on a shooting rampage in the Polish city of Krakow on Saturday has died two days after being critically wounded by officers, police said on Monday.
"We inform you that the perpetrator of the tragic events died this morning in the hospital," regional police said in a post on X.
The man drove past the square in Krakow's Old Town, an area of Poland's second-largest city visited by many tourists, and carried out the shooting. He continued shooting even after suffering wounds by police officers, according to the authorities.
He is also suspected of killing his parents and sister at his family home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles), before carrying out the alleged attack in central Krakow.
Six people were killed and 15 wounded in the shooting spree by the 24-year-old Polish man who allegedly carried out the attack.
The victims were of various nationalities. Three women and one man were Polish, with two other victims being an Austrian woman and a British man. The list of people injured includes people from Britain, Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.
The two officers who stopped the assailant also remained in hospital.
Poland in mourning
The shooting is being investigated as a terrorist offense. While Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said the assailant held radical and ultranationalist views, no information has been given as to whether he was a member of any extremist organization.
Grief and shock took over Poland after the shooting.
The attack's site at the city's central square became a place of commemoration as many people laid candles and flowers.
The St. Mary's Trumpet Call, the melody played at Krakow's Main Square every hour, stopped in honor of the victims. This was the first time this happened since World War II. The St. Anne's Church received a wave of mourners who came to attend a service for the victims.
Mass shootings are not common in Poland. Some 411,000 hold gun permits across the country, with interest in gun ownership being on the rise. Poland mourns victims of Krakow mass shootingTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

sources.headline: Poland: Tusk and Nawrocki honour six victims of Kraków shooting
sources.text:
Updated: 9 November 2026 - 22:34 GMT+1
Poland's President and Prime Minister set aside their political differences to honour the six victims of a deadly shooting in Kraków. The two leaders laid candles and knelt together at a vigil in the historic city centre.
The two political rivals arrived together at the memorial, where Tusk held a candle as a uniformed officer played a horn nearby. They then placed candles among those left in memory of the victims before kneeling side by side in a moment of remembrance. Nawrocki repeatedly made the sign of the cross as the two leaders paid their respects. Footage shows rows of flickering candles, mourners gathered at the site and a Polish flag, reflecting the grief following Saturday's attack, which also left 15 people injured.
The rare public appearance together comes amid a bitter political dispute between Tusk and Nawrocki over reforms to Poland's Constitutional Tribunal. Despite their disagreements, both leaders took part in the ceremony honouring those killed in the 7 November shooting.
The attack in the heart of Kraków, one of Poland's best-known historic cities, had triggered scenes of panic as people fled the gunfire. In the days since, residents have returned to the area to light candles and pay their respects, while bullet marks remain visible on nearby café windows. Monday's vigil brought the country's two most prominent political figures together in a shared tribute to the victims, offering a moment of unity despite their continuing political differences.

sources.headline: Thousands participate in silent march after Krakow mass shooting that shocked the nation
sources.text: WARSAW - Thousands of people took part in a silent march through Krakow on the evening of Nov 9 along with Poland’s president and prime minister as the country tries to come to terms with an unprecedented mass shooting, in which a Polish man killed six people on the southern city’s main square.Relations between Prime Minister Donald Tusk and President Karol Nawrocki are tense, but they appear to want a display of national unity over an incident that has shocked Poland and left rival political camps bitterly disputing the killer’s motives.“For Poland, this is always a sign of hope: that while we may hold different views, we are still capable of cooperating, engaging in dialogue, and seeking out what unites us,” Deputy Prime Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told TVN24.“We are capable of showing solidarity during difficult times. Together, we can support those who need such support,” he added.March participants followed part of the route the shooter drove while firing and lit memorial candles at the spots where people were killed on Nov 7.“Tonight in Cracow thousands of Poles gathered to pay tribute to the victims of November 7 attack,” Tusk wrote on X.The suspected gunman died in hospital on Nov 9 after being shot and arrested by police minutes after they said he opened fire from his car in Krakow’s historic main square, a popular tourist destination.The government said the man, identified by prosecutors as 24-year-old Michal Oksinski from the south-eastern town of Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, may have been inspired by far-right ideology. But officials appeared to backtrack on Nov 9.“Until the matter is fully clarified and the authorities are in possession of complete information, it is best to refrain from making comments, even if there are some initial indications,” government spokesperson Adam Szlapka told TVN24.Both the shooter and his father held gun permits, and several firearms were found in the family apartment and the assailant’s car, prosecutors said.The bodies of his father, mother and sister were found in their family home on Nov 7, and officials say they were also likely killed by Oksinski.Dispute over killer’s motivesThe nationalist opposition rejected the suggestion of a far-right link to the killings, with Law and Justice party leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski saying those claims were a “blatant lie.”People gather for a silent march at the Main Market Square in Krakow, Poland, on Nov 9. PHOTO: REUTERSNational Prosecutor’s Office spokesperson Przemyslaw Nowak told a press conference that investigators did not yet know what motivated the killer.He said that a yellow flag featuring a snake and the words “Don’t tread on me,” known as the Gadsden flag, was found in Oksinski’s room.The Gadsden flag was first used during the American Revolution in the 18th century. Nowak said the flag was associated with “various meanings related to freedom or rebellion” but was not widely known as being linked to any form of extremism.Interior Ministry spokesperson Karolina Galecka said there were many different emblems on the perpetrator’s clothing that had already been partially examined and interpreted.Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek said despite the death of the shooter, the investigation would continue, and would aim to establish if he acted alone or was inspired by any group.“Evidence is being collected, but I will not show or disclose it. I ask for restraint,” Zurek told Radio Zet.Poland’s Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime (CBZC) said it had detained five Polish citizens and one Ukrainian who had posted threatening or alarming content online following the attack. It said the detainees were aged 15 to 36.Galecka said the CBZC and the police were on high alert for potential copycats.Nation in shockPoland had never experienced such a mass shooting. Scenes of blood and bodies strewn across the historic heart of one of its main tourist attractions have shocked a nation that has long viewed itself as safer than Western European neighbours that have experienced similar attacks.“A total of four firearms and several hundred rounds of ammunition were discovered in the vehicle and in the possession of Michal Oksinski,” Nowak said.“We secured a very large number of spent casings. In total, at least several dozen shots were fired — possibly even several hundred.”Nowak said the two police officers injured in the attack had regained consciousness.Tusk wrote on X that when police officer Artur Moranski woke up, his first words were, “Is Kuba alive?” — referring to fellow injured officer Jakub Kulik.The government will review regulations on requirements for people with gun permits following the tragedy, Zurek said. REUTERS

Poland in shock after 6 killed in Krakow far-right shooting

Issued on: 08/11/2026 - 15:21
Modified: 08/11/2026 - 16:27

Poland on Sunday launched a terror probe into the mass shooting in Krakow the day before, in which six people were killed and many more were injured. Authorities have said that the 24-year-old suspect, who used a semi-automatic rifle in his killing spree, was “fascinated by far-right ideologies”. He is currently in critical condition in hospital. FRANCE 24 journalist Adrien Sariat reports from Poland.

sources.headline: Poland treats fatal mass shooting as 'terrorist offence'
sources.text: Polish prosecutors say a mass shooting that killed six people and injured at least 15 others is being treated as an act "constituting a terrorist offence".The attack, which Poland's defence minister described as an "act of terror," happened on Saturday, local time, in the Main Square in the heart of Krakow's Old Town.The square is a major tourist hub in the country's second-largest city.Polish police guarded Krakow's Main Square more than a day after the shooting. (Reuters: Jakub Porzyck)Four women and two men were killed in the shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, according to Malopolska regional governor Krzysztof Jan Klęczar.A man from the United Kingdom and a woman from Austria were also among the dead, authorities said.A video posted on social media showed a police officer repeatedly shooting the attacker, who was lying on the street. The officer later slowly collapsed to the ground.Poland has entered two days of national mourning. (Reuters: Jakub Porzycki)The two police officers who stopped the gunman, in actions authorities hailed as heroic, remain in hospital. They were both conscious by Sunday afternoon.The bodies of the assailant's sister, mother and father were also found at the man's family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometres north-east of Krakow. They likely died from gunshot wounds.The square reopened on Sunday evening, with mourners gathering to lay flowers and candles in honour of the victims.Poland has entered two days of national mourning.St. Mary's Trumpet Call, a traditional five-note melody which played every hour from the highest tower of St Mary's Basilica, was paused overnight — the first time the call had been missed since World War II.Witnesses recall moments of chaosMarie-Ange Collaer wrote on Facebook that she and her family survived the shooting during a trip to Krakow from Brussels."We literally ran for our lives and managed to hide from the bullets flying around," she wrote."Lying on the floor in a shop like in a bad police movie whilst you hear bullets everywhere."British resident Neil Thaxton and his wife also lived through the attack."We had just walked through the main square and heard the gunshots," he wrote on Facebook."We thought it was fireworks then people started running, we went into a gift shop and the staff took us in the back of the shop and locked the doors and turned the lights off."Witnesses who survived the shooting say they scrambled to find refuge in nearby stores. (Reuters: Jakub Porzycki)Alexandros Maronitis, a tourist from Greece, told The Associated Press that he could not get back to his lodgings for five hours after the shooting."We saw the shooter when they picked him up with the ambulance," he said."So, we're a bit afraid. It's our first time in Poland. We heard it's a safe country."Krakow's St Anne's Church was packed with people who attended a memorial service. (AP: Jakub Porzycki)Witness Andy Hill told the BBC he felt as though he was in a movie scene."It doesn't feel real," he said."And the trouble is, you have such an instantaneous moment to make a decision: Run. Stand still. There's an element of shock. But I just thought the easiest thing to do is dive through a doorway and just take refuge behind the windows."Grim first for PolandPoland's Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect held "very radical" and "ultranationalistic" views."Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," he said at a news conference on Saturday.Local officials in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski said they seized seven weapons from the family home, bringing the total number recovered to 11, including four found on the suspect or in his car in Krakow.Both father and son had gun permits, they said.The suspect, a Polish citizen, remains in a critical condition after undergoing multiple surgeries.There was confusion on Saturday about his age, with authorities first saying 24 and later 25. On Sunday they confirmed he was 24.The suspect's dead sibling was a young artist studying at the Krakow Academy of Fine Arts."Nothing will ever be like before. The delicate tissue of our academic community was painfully wounded," the academy wrote in a statement on Sunday.A shooting club in Starachowice, where the suspect is believed to have trained, said it only offered "static shooting". (Reuters: Kacper Pempel)The academy confirmed Magdalena Oksińska was a third year student and that, additionally, the sister of an academy employee was shot twice."Magdalena Oksińska, 21 years old, a queer person, was an absolutely talented painter, photographer, poet and writer," architect Pavko Krajka wrote in a post on social media, accompanied by images of the artist's colourful paintings.About 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising.The Swit shooting club in Starachowice, where the suspect is believed to have trained, issued a statement on Sunday saying it offered only "static shooting," which involves firing from a fixed position at a stationary target.The club said the suspect "was never trained in our club in the areas of dynamic, tactical or combat shooting".Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland, however, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many injured, including children.The Krakow shooter's military gear, guns and overall look were similar to those of other "extreme right lone actors" committing attacks around Europe, said Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague."We have had attempts before, but now we can say that these kinds of attacks have become successful in Poland," he said.AP
